reading.en:
The accuracy of machine translation is rising rapidly. Point your smartphone at a sign while travelling and Japanese appears instantly. Put a work email through translation software and you get an almost flawless text. It is natural, then, to wonder whether there is any point in spending time and effort learning a foreign language.
I have taught Spanish at university for over twenty years. Recently students have more often asked me, 'Why do we have to learn grammar when there are translation apps?' To be honest, I could not answer right away, because if it is just exchanging information, there are many situations where leaving it to a machine is faster and more accurate.
However, hearing one international student's story helped me sort out my thoughts. When she had just come to Japan, she managed to live using a translation app. But even after six months she had no Japanese friends. Conversation worked through the app, but she could not laugh together over jokes or sense each other's unspoken feelings. She only truly made friends after she started speaking in her own Japanese, however clumsy.
Language is a tool for carrying information, and at the same time something that builds relationships between people. The effort to speak in the other person's language is itself a message: 'I want to know you.' Even full of mistakes, that effort reaches the other person. However accurately a machine translates, it cannot replace this part.
Furthermore, learning a foreign language also means looking again at your own language. In Spanish, you use two kinds of 'you' depending on your distance from the other person. Students who learn this start to think again about Japanese keigo. Through contact with the system of another language, they realize that their own language and way of thinking, which they took for granted, are actually just one way of seeing things.
Progress in translation technology should be welcomed. I use it a lot when travelling. But judging the value of foreign language study only by the efficiency of conveying information is far too narrow a view. Now I would answer the student like this: 'An app will speak for you. But it won't make friends for you.'

A: Some primary schools are getting rid of homework. I support this. Family situations vary: some parents can help with homework, others come home late from work and cannot. It has been pointed out that homework is one cause of widening gaps in ability due to home environment. Also, children need time to play and to be with their families. Isn't the proper way that what should be learned at school is finished at school?

B: I have doubts about abolishing homework across the board. The habit of sitting at a desk on your own every day, even a little, becomes the foundation for continuing to learn by yourself in the future. It is true that families differ in how much they can support their children's study. But in that case, homework can be made something children can do alone, or a place can be set up at school after class to work on assignments. Isn't the problem not homework itself, but its content and how it is given?

reading.en:
These days, when we try to look something up, something like an 'answer' appears within seconds of searching. From cooking steps to symptoms of illness to relationship worries, someone has already prepared an answer. Without noticing, we have come to think it natural to get an answer as soon as we ask a question.
But is that really so? Many problems in the world have no single right answer in the first place. What job to choose, how to deal with family, how to tackle local issues. Applying someone else's answer as it is to such questions will not necessarily work, because no two situations, and no two sets of people involved, are the same.
Nevertheless, we can no longer bear having no answer. When there is something we don't know, we get anxious and jump at the nearest answer for now. If that answer doesn't fit, we look for another. As we consume answers one after another like this, isn't the work of thinking with our own heads being left behind?
What I think is important is the ability to stay in a state of 'not knowing'. Not giving an answer right away, but holding on to the question and turning it over in your mind. As you talk with people and gain experience, your own answer gradually takes shape. An answer gained that way, even if incomplete, should be far more reliable than one borrowed from others.
Of course, there are situations where you should know the answer right away. When someone suddenly falls ill there is no time to think at leisure. An environment where information can be obtained quickly is itself a great benefit. The problem is treating every question the same way. Telling apart questions that need speed from questions that deserve time: I think that is exactly the wisdom required of us who live in an age overflowing with information.

listening.en: Expert: Here are four ways to improve sleep quality. First, take a lukewarm bath an hour before bed. Second, don't look at your smartphone before bed. Third, get up at the same time every morning, including holidays. Fourth, do light exercise in the evening. M: I sleep until noon on days off, so I'll start by fixing that.
